exploring indias ancient rock paintings techniques pigments and conservation challenges x200b introduction rock paintings represent one of the most enduring forms of human expression capturing the essence of prehistoric and ancient societies through vivid imagery etched onto natural canvases in india these artworks span thousands of years offering a window into the creative efforts and cultural practices of early inhabitants as diverse as the nations landscapes rock paintings are found in various regions from the dense forests of central india to the arid hills of the south they depict scenes of daily life hunting rituals and mythical narratives using techniques that have fascinated archaeologists and historians alike this review delves into the technical aspects of these paintings including the pigments employed the methods of application and the ongoing efforts to conserve them against the ravages of time and environment the significance of indian rock paintings lies not only in their artistic value but also in their role as historical documents discovered in the mid19th century these sites have revealed much about prehistoric human behavior social structures and environmental interactions for instance the paintings often illustrate animals human figures and geometric patterns suggesting a deep connection to nature and spirituality over the years extensive research has been conducted leading to a better understanding of their creation and the challenges in preserving them this exploration aims to provide a comprehensive overview highlighting the ingenuity of ancient artists and the modern strategies to safeguard this heritage historical discovery and significance the journey into indias rock art began in the 19th century when british archaeologists and explorers stumbled upon these hidden treasures one of the earliest documented discoveries was in 1867 by archibald carlleyle who uncovered paintings in rock shelters in the mirzapur region of uttar pradesh his findings sparked interest in the prehistoric art forms that predated known civilizations following this in 1879 j cockburn reported similar artworks in the kaimur hills further expanding the known scope these initial revelations were pivotal as they challenged prevailing notions about the antiquity of human settlement in the subcontinent by the early 20th century more systematic surveys were undertaken in 1932 frank brown documented sites in the raigarh district noting the stylistic variations that hinted at different cultural phases the postindependence era saw a surge in indianled research with scholars like vs wakankar making groundbreaking contributions wakankars discovery of the bhimbetka rock shelters in 1957 marked a turning point located in madhya pradesh bhimbetka boasts over 700 shelters with paintings dating back to the mesolithic period around 10000 years ago recognized as a unesco world heritage site in 2003 it exemplifies the richness of indias rock art heritage the significance of these paintings extends beyond mere aesthetics they serve as anthropological records illustrating the evolution of human societies for example early paintings often feature large animals like elephants and bison symbolizing hunting practices and reverence for wildlife later artworks incorporate more complex scenes including dances battles and agricultural activities reflecting societal advancements in regions like kerala and tamil nadu rock art connects to dravidian cultures while northern sites link to indoaryan influences this art form also provides insights into prehistoric technology such as the use of natural resources for pigments demonstrating early chemical knowledge moreover rock paintings have influenced modern interpretations of indian history they challenge eurocentric views by showcasing advanced artistic traditions predating those in europe comparisons with global rock art such as the lascaux caves in france or altamira in spain reveal similarities in themes but unique regional adaptations in india the paintings continuity from paleolithic to historic times underscores a cultural thread that weaves through millennia informing contemporary discussions on heritage and identity geographical distribution indias vast and varied terrain hosts rock paintings in numerous locations each with distinct characteristics shaped by local geology and climate central india particularly madhya pradesh is a hotspot with bhimbetka being the most prominent this site nestled in the vindhya hills features paintings in quartzite shelters that have protected them from erosion nearby sites like adamgarh and panchmarhi offer similar depictions often in red and white hues portraying hunting scenes and human figures moving north uttar pradesh harbors significant clusters in the mirzapur and banda districts the lakhania and wyndham falls shelters display artworks from the mesolithic era with motifs of animals and geometric designs in bihar the kaimur hills reveal paintings that blend prehistoric and later influences including buddhist symbols rajasthans contributions include sites in the bhanpurachambal region where paintings on sandstone surfaces depict wildlife and rituals southern india presents a different palette in karnataka the badami and hampi areas feature rock art on granite outcrops often associated with megalithic cultures keralas edakkal cave discovered in 1895 contains petroglyphs and paintings that may date back 6000 years showing humananimal interactions tamil nadus sites such as those in the nilgiri hills include engravings alongside paintings hinting at ritualistic purposes eastern regions like odisha and jharkhand also contribute in odisha the ushakothi and vikramkhol sites showcase vivid red ochre paintings of elephants and deer jharkhands hazaribagh district is known for its khoj or search paintings depicting community hunts western india including gujarat and maharashtra has fewer but notable sites such as the pavagadh hill in gujarat with paintings from the chalcolithic period this distribution is not random it correlates with ancient human migration routes and resource availability shelters were chosen for their natural protection often near water sources facilitating longterm habitation mapping these sites reveals patterns of cultural diffusion with stylistic similarities suggesting interactions between regions for instance the use of stick figures in central india mirrors those in southern sites indicating shared artistic conventions painting techniques ancient indian artists employed a range of techniques to create enduring rock paintings adapting to available materials and environmental conditions one prominent method was the spray color technique documented in various sites this involved blowing pigment through a tube often made from hollow bones or reeds to produce fine even layers wakankars 1978 study highlights its use in creating translucent effects where pigments were diluted in water or binders for a ethereal appearance transparent techniques were common in early periods allowing the rocks natural texture to show through pigments were applied in thin washes creating depth and luminosity in contrast opaque methods used thicker pastes for bold solid colors seen in later historic paintings these techniques required precise control as the irregular rock surfaces posed challenges another approach was the use of finger painting or direct application with hands evident in sites like bhimbetka artists would dip fingers into pigment mixtures and draw outlines or fill areas adding a personal touch stenciling where hands or objects were placed against the wall and pigment blown around them created negative images a technique shared with australian aboriginal art petroglyphs or carvings sometimes complemented paintings in kerala engravings were filled with pigments for enhanced visibility the combination of incising and painting allowed for intricate details such as in animal fur or human adornments these methods evolved over time with mesolithic art favoring simple lines and chalcolithic periods introducing more complex compositions the choice of technique often depended on the rock type quartzite abundant in central india provided a smooth canvas for fine details while granite in the south required coarser applications artists demonstrated remarkable adaptability using natural contours to integrate artworks into the landscape enhancing their symbolic power materials used pigments and binders the vibrancy of indian rock paintings stems from natural pigments derived from minerals plants and animals red hues the most prevalent came from hematite iron oxide sourced from local deposits this pigment known for its stability was ground into powder and mixed with binders yellows originated from limonite or ochre while blacks were from manganese dioxide or charcoal whites used kaolin or lime and greens from glauconite or plant extracts chemical analyses reveal the sophistication in pigment selection for instance red ochres iron content provides durability against fading in some sites rare blues from lapis lazuli indicate trade networks pigments were prepared by grinding with stones then suspended in media for application binders were crucial for adhesion organic materials like animal fat blood or plant resins acted as glues blood rich in proteins formed a sticky medium when mixed with pigments plant saps such as from acacia trees provided viscosity in southern sites honey or egg whites might have been used drawing parallels with tempera techniques these materials natural origins ensured harmony with the environment but also vulnerability to degradation modern studies using spectroscopy confirm the use of these compounds offering insights into ancient chemistry the selection reflected not just availability but symbolic meaningsred for life black for deathembedding cultural narratives in the art tools and application methods prehistoric artists crafted tools from available resources to apply pigments precisely brushes were made from animal hair feathers or plant fibers bound to sticks with resins squirrel or goat hair provided fine tips for details while broader brushes from porcupine quills covered larger areas application methods varied wet techniques involved mixing pigments with water for fluid strokes ideal for flowing lines dry methods used powdered pigments rubbed directly onto surfaces creating textured effects in humid climates artists exploited moisture to blend colors seamlessly tools also included spatulas from bones for spreading pastes and sharpened sticks for incising outlines before painting in group settings multiple artists might collaborate using scaffolds for high shelters these methods highlight ingenuity turning rudimentary implements into instruments of lasting art causes of deterioration despite their longevity rock paintings face numerous threats natural causes include water seepage which dissolves binders and causes flaking wind erosion abrades surfaces while temperature fluctuations lead to cracking biological factors like lichen growth obscure artworks and bat guanos acidity corrodes pigments humaninduced deterioration is equally severe vandalism such as graffiti defaces sites and tourism increases exposure to humidity from breaths development projects like dams flood shelters altering microclimates pollution from industries deposits harmful chemicals accelerating fading climatic changes exacerbate these issues increased rainfall in central india leads to more seepage while droughts crack rocks understanding these causes is vital for targeted conservation conservation strategies conservation begins with documentation using photography and 3d scanning to record sites chemical stabilization involves applying consolidants like acrylic resins to bind flaking pigments environmental controls such as barriers against water protect shelters biological treatments remove lichens with safe biocides followed by preventive measures community involvement educates locals on heritage value reducing vandalism international collaborations bring advanced techniques ensuring sustainable preservation conclusion indias rock paintings encapsulate millennia of human creativity facing modern challenges that demand concerted conservation by understanding their techniques and threats we can ensure their survival for future generations sources 1 jhum cultivation in colonial assam indigenous traditions and colonial interventions introduction jhum cultivation often referred to as shifting or swidden agriculture represents one of the oldest and most enduring forms of farming practiced by indigenous communities across various regions of the world particularly in tropical and subtropical hilly terrains in the context of colonial assam which encompassed the presentday states of assam meghalaya mizoram nagaland and parts of neighboring areas jhum was not merely a method of subsistence but a deeply ingrained cultural and economic practice that sustained tribal societies for millennia this system involved clearing patches of forest burning the vegetation to enrich the soil with ash cultivating crops for a few seasons and then allowing the land to regenerate under fallow periods before returning to it the practice was ideally suited to the regions heavy rainfall steep slopes and dense forests where permanent ploughbased agriculture was often impractical due to soil erosion and nutrient depletion the historical significance of jhum can be traced back to the neolithic era around 8000 bce when human societies transitioned from huntergatherer lifestyles to settled food production in india particularly in the northeastern hills jhum has remained a dominant mode of agriculture supporting millions of households even today colonial records from the british era frequently mention jhum as the primary cultivation method in hilly districts for instance early gazetteers described it as the ordinary method in the hills emphasizing its prevalence among tribes like the garos khasis lushais and mikirs the term jhum itself is derived from local assamese and tribal languages but equivalents exist across india and beyond podu in odisha dahi in madhya pradesh kumri in karnataka and taungya in burma all denoting variations of slashandburn farming this article explores the intricacies of jhum as an indigenous practice in colonial assam and examines the british colonial administrations attitudes and policies toward it the british viewed jhum through the lens of their imperial interests which prioritized commercial exploitation of forests for timber railways and shipbuilding they often labeled it as primitive or wasteful seeking to restrict or ban it to expand plantations and assert control over forest resources however indigenous communities resisted these impositions viewing jhum as integral to their way of life the conflict led to compromises such as the adoption of the taungya system which blended cultivation with forestry drawing from empirical and historical methods this analysis relies on primary sources like forest administration reports district gazetteers and official records from archives alongside secondary literature on colonial ecology and tribal economies the study highlights how jhum was adapted to local ecosystems providing food security in remote areas while maintaining ecological balance through long fallow cycles yet under colonial pressures shortened cycles due to population growth and land restrictions led to degradation fueling debates on its sustainability by delving into the process cultural significance scholarly debates and british responses this article underscores the tensions between indigenous knowledge systems and colonial modernization efforts in assam the process of jhum cultivation the mechanics of jhum cultivation in colonial assam were finely tuned to the regions environmental conditions involving a cyclical process that balanced human needs with natural regeneration the origin of this practice remains shrouded in antiquity but evidence suggests it was widespread among tribal groups long before colonial contact in assams hills communities such as the garos khasis and lushais depended on jhum for their primary livelihood with an estimated 5 million tribal families across india practicing it on over 4 million hectares of land during the colonial period the process typically began with site selection conducted by village elders or clan leaders between october and december plots were chosen on hillsides or in jungles often allocating half to one hectare per family clearing commenced in january or february where secondary bamboo forests or undergrowth were slashed leaving larger tree stumps intact to prevent soil erosion and support climbing crops this partial clearing was a key adaptation as complete deforestation would exacerbate landslides in the steep terrain drying of the slashed vegetation followed lasting until march or april when it was burned the burning phase was critical it eliminated weeds and pests while the resulting ash acted as a natural fertilizer enriching the soil with nutrients like potassium and phosphorus colonial observers noted the laborintensive nature of this work performed with traditional tools like daos machetes and hoes in the garo hills for example villagers felled woody growth in october reserving poles for construction or sale and burned the rest in march fires were carefully controlled to avoid spreading into adjacent forests with communities like the garos imposing fines on villages responsible for uncontrolled blazes sowing occurred with the onset of rains in april involving a mix of crops such as paddy maize vegetables tubers and cotton this polyculture approach maximized yields and minimized risks from pests or weather variability the land was hoed lightly without deep ploughing to preserve soil structure crops were harvested over one to three seasons after which the plot was left fallow for 10 to 25 years to allow regeneration during fallow secondary vegetation like bamboo or coppice shoots reclaimed the area restoring fertility bamboo in particular served as a soil binder facilitating nutrient recovery and creating microhabitats for biodiversity variations existed across districts in the lushai hills bamboodominated plots could be recultivated every four to five years without depleting the bamboo allowing chiefs to alternate between village sites in contrast treeheavy jungles required longer fallows as repeated burning could lead to grass invasion rendering the land useless per local beliefs indigenous techniques for erosion control included laying logs across slopes in staggered patterns as practiced by the khasis or leaving charred trunks to form fences against animals like deer rats and elephants temporary huts in tree forks provided vigilance against wildlife this process was sustainable when fallow periods were adequate as the ecosystem recovered fully however colonial encroachments on forests shortened cycles leading to reduced productivity jhummias demonstrated profound seasonal knowledge burning signaled the approaching monsoon and ashes washed downhill enriched lowland fields creating an unintended symbiotic relationship with settled farmers overall jhums efficiency in highrainfall lowsoilfertility areas made it superior to introduced methods explaining its persistence despite colonial critiques jhum as an integral part of indigenous culture beyond its agricultural utility jhum cultivation was woven into the fabric of indigenous social economic and cultural life in colonial assam for tribal communities it was a way of life that encompassed rituals community bonds and economic selfsufficiency in regions like the garo khasi and jaintia hills where 85 of cultivated land was under jhum it served as the economic mainstay supporting rural populations in inaccessible areas culturally jhum was linked to rituals and festivals many tribes performed ceremonies during site selection burning and harvesting to invoke blessings for bountiful yields in meghalaya jhum remained a cultural emblem integral to identity and folklore the practice fostered communal labor clearing and burning often involved the entire village reinforcing social ties land allocation by elders ensured equitable distribution preventing conflicts and promoting collective responsibility economically jhum provided diverse outputsrice cotton vegetables and tubersensuring food security without reliance on markets the fallow system allowed soil recuperation sustaining longterm productivity in garo communities secondyear crops like yams and chilies supplemented diets while fallows regenerated timber for housing and fuel this selfreliant model contrasted with colonial cashcrop economies which prioritized exports over local needs environmental adaptations underscored cultural ingenuity techniques like partial clearing and log barriers minimized erosion reflecting generations of ecological knowledge reserved trees shaded crops and prevented soil loss while fences and snares managed wildlife jhums superiority in assams climateheavy rains and acidic soilslay in its organic approach avoiding chemical inputs that could harm biodiversity however population pressures and colonial land grabs disrupted this harmony shortened fallows led to degradation but indigenous views held that proper cycles maintained balance scholars note that jhum conserved soil nutrients through weed cover and supported wildlife by allowing forest regrowth in essence jhum embodied a holistic worldview where agriculture harmonized with nature culture and community resisting colonial attempts to commodify land debates on the impacts of shifting cultivation the scholarly discourse on jhum cultivation in colonial assam reveals polarized views on its environmental and social effects critics often aligned with colonial perspectives decried it as destructive while proponents highlighted its sustainability and cultural value detractors argued that jhum caused deforestation soil erosion and reduced productivity forest officers noted thousands of square miles turned barren annually linking it to landslides river silting and floods they viewed it as primitive incompatible with scientific forestry which aimed to maximize timber yields this narrative justified colonial interventions portraying jhum as wasteful compared to permanent agriculture conversely modern studies affirm jhums suitability for assams ecosystems it provides food security in remote areas conserves soil through fallows and enhances biodiversity weed management retains moisture and nutrients while erosion under jhum is often less than in terraced farming wildlife benefits from regenerating forests with species surviving long cycles in humid tropics jhum mimics natural disturbances promoting resilience in assam the rainforest climate favored jhum over monocultures which depleted soils faster traditional practices were less destructive than colonial logging debates underscore how colonial biases framed jhum as backward ignoring its adaptive genius ultimately sustainability hinged on cycle length shortened periods under colonialism amplified negatives but indigenous management proved effective british colonial attitudes and policies toward jhum british attitudes toward jhum in colonial assam evolved from curiosity to hostility driven by economic imperatives initially officials documented it neutrally but as demands for timber grewfor railways ships and tea plantationsthey sought to curb it foresters blamed jhum for forest loss imposing restrictions like double taxes on migrating villages or site changes regulations in 1874 penalized shifts aiming to sedentarize tribes vigilance in reserves like nambor and golaghat involved guards and warnings to prevent trespassing fines and evictions were common with tribes like the kukis confined to marked areas resistance was fierce villagers objected to planting timber fearing loss of jhum rights revenue officers advocated moderation recognizing jhums revenue potential and tribal hardships this led to experiments like distributing teak seeds but uptake was low the 1891 sylhet jhum regulation claimed state rights over shifting lands restricting cultivation in open forests chiefs like archdale earle pushed for abolition deeming it wasteful but acknowledged its cultural hold demarcation reduced jhumming in reserves but unclassed forests saw continuation compromise emerged in taungya borrowed from burma allowing crops amid timber plantations introduced in the 1880s it reduced weeding costs and provided livelihoods in nowgong villagers cropped between planted lines for free taungya reconciled forestry and agriculture though conflicts arose over tree vigor and weed suppression british confusionforesters versus revenue officershighlighted policy inconsistencies while forests were prioritized for profit tribal welfare concerns tempered outright bans taungyas success ironically reintroduced jhum elements affirming indigenous methods viability conclusion jhum cultivation in colonial assam exemplified indigenous ingenuity adapting to challenging terrains while sustaining communities culturally and economically despite british efforts to suppress it for commercial gains its resilience led to hybrid systems like taungya this interplay reveals colonial exploitations limits against local traditions mangled carcasses of mammoths woolly rhinos sabretoothed cats and bison lie jumbled with tree trunks and peat the condition of the remainsflashfrozen while alive broken bones unnatural posturesindicates not a gradual extinction but a sudden and violent death entire islands in the arctic ocean such as kotelny island consist of animal bones swept from the continent by a monstrous tectonic activity changes in sea level and possibly shifts in the magnetic poles all of this paints a picture of a brief but exceptionally powerful blow to earths biosphere and geology particularly affecting the northern hemisphere possible causes from glacial seas to cosmic impacts scientists and researchers propose several hypotheses each attempting to explain a piece of the puzzle while facing its own complexities 1 glacial floods according to the theory popularized by researcher graham hancock the cause could have been the catastrophic breach of giant proglacial lakes at the end of the last ice age melting ice led to the formation of vast reservoirs like lake agassiz in north america when natural ice dams collapsed colossal waves of water tens to hundreds of meters high surged onto the continents sweeping away everything in their path this could explain the formation of mammoth cemeteries along the shores of the arctic ocean however for a global catastrophe a chain of nearly simultaneous breaches worldwide is required as well as a cause for such rapid and synchronous ice melting 2 the cosmic hypothesis comet or asteroid impact this version developed in particular by scientists richard firestone and allen west suggests that around 12800 years ago a fragment of a large comet struck earth exploding in the atmosphere over north america the consequences included massive fires a shockwave the ejection of dust that blocked the sun and the onset of a sharp coolingthe younger dryas supporting this are findings in the geological layers of that time of microscopic crustal displacement an idea proposed by charles hapgood and supported by albert einstein suggests the possibility of the entire earths crust rapidly sliding over the mantle due to mass imbalance from or galactic activity a number of researchers such as douglas vogt or paul laviolette see the cause in an external energy impact on the solar system this could have been a powerful coronal mass everyday life and activities of a later stone age community at beefa cave melka kunture upper awash ethiopia introduction the definition of the later stone age in the horn of africa is undeniably problematic as it lacks a welldefined chronological technological and cultural framework in other regions of the continent for example in north africa the transition between the middle stone age msa and the later stone age lsa corresponds neatly with changes in lithic technology ie a transition from levalloisbased lithic assemblages to bladebasemicrolithic ones and shifts in paleoclimate and paleoenvironment however the situation in the horn of africa is more complicated several authors have acknowledged that current evidence does not always support a distinction between a levalloisbased msa lacking bladelets and microliths and a geometric microlithsbased lsa where the levallois technique is not present anymore clark 1997 tryon 2019 spinapolice 2020 pazan et al 2023 there is however a general agreement about the significant technotypological variability of lsa industries often characterized by microliths although microliths make their first appearance much earlier mnard 2015 lplongeon et al 2017 in clarks reconstruction 1954 the most recent phase of the local msa the somaliland stillbay already presents some of the lithic tools and technologies usually associated with lsa lithic assemblages backed flakes burins and pressure knapping this phase is followed in the whole region by at least four transitional msalsa phases somaliland magosian hargesian doian and somaliland wilton which are characterized by the presence of microliths pressure knapping backed bladelets burins endscrapers and arrowheads according to brandt 1986 early holocene microlithic assemblages appear between 12000 and 5000 bp and the earliest pottery is associated with site fejx2 in the ethiopian highlands following the msa the lsa in the horn of africa spans a broad chronological period from approximately 40 ka to the midholocene overlapping in the last period with the appearance of food production at pastoral sites brandt 1986 pleurdeau et al 2014 mnard 2015 consequently the more recent phases of the stone age of the horn should be put in broader perspective the increasing availability of newly excavated and dated sites is crucial for clarifying both chronological and paleoenvironmental aspects of human occupation between the latefinal pleistocene and the earlymidholocene at regional and topographic levels understanding changes in settlement systems and their relationships to climatic shifts can contribute to drawing a clear general framework for the lsa in the horn of africa if we consider the increased presence of microliths as an essential feature of lsa lithic assemblages we need to clearly define them therefore it is necessary to consider the wide variety of microlith types that can fall within this class of artifacts three elements are usually considered characteristic of the microlithic package backing miniaturization and microblade production which however can also be independently present clarkson et al 2018 even though microliths are often smaller than 3 cm and can have a geometric shape burdukiewicz 2005 they are not necessarily limited to miniature formal tools microliths can also refer to crescents segments and lunates of bigger size leplongeon 2014 also in both africa and eurasia microliths are often linked to bladeletbased lithic complexes and microburin techniques peresani miolo 2012 goldstein shaffer 2017 the production of microliths from small flakes via retouch is also somewhat common belfercohen gorringmorris 2002 sari 2022 moreover the variability of lsa assemblages in the horn of africa may have various explanations a considerable time span from 40 ka to 5 ka that may have encapsulated substantial behavioral change substantial climatic shifts that may have structured aspects of this change geographical and geomorphological variability elevation vegetation humidity proximity to lakes etc that may have impacted past human activity raw material availability and mechanical properties that may have shaped how tools were made used and discarded and site function ie sites from the same behavioral system may have preserved very different archaeological signatures following leplongeon and colleagues 2017 we approach this problem by integrating a comparative observation of lithic attributes with an analysis of the chane opratoire to understand at high resolution the technological knowhow of specific human groups in this paper we present preliminary data from the lsa site of beefa cave in the ethiopian highlands we infer that beefa cave like other lsa sites was occupied by huntergatherers from the final pleistocene to the midholocene at which point groups of neolithic pastoralists reliant on sheep goats and cattle began to flourish

lighting means shells ropes and anchors everywhere in reality the most successful coastalinspired lighting schemes are quite restrained they borrow from the colours textures and natural light of the coast rather than copying obvious seaside motifs at its core coastal lighting is about three things softness direction and material softness comes from how the light is diffused coastal interiors rarely feel harsh or clinical instead they feel like an overcast day at the beach bright enough to function but gentle on the eyes you can create this with fixtures that have shades in glass fabric or frosted finishes and by avoiding bare glaring bulbs in key living areas direction is about how the light is aimed spaces that feel flat are often lit only from the ceiling usually with one bright central fixture a coastalinspired space uses layers you still have general ceiling lighting but it is supported by wall lights table or floor lamps and sometimes subtle accent lighting this layering mimics the way natural light moves in from multiple directions through windows and reflections material is what most people notice first coastal lighting often uses finishes like brushed metal weathered wood rattan light ceramics and clear or seeded glass the trick is balance one rattan pendant in a kitchen can feel fresh and coastal five different beachy elements in one room can quickly feel cluttered future lights team often describes it to homeowners like this choose lighting that looks like it belongs in a bright airy space even if your room does not feel that way yet the fixtures then help you move the room in that direction if you live in a coastal city or a humid climate there is also a practical side salt air humidity and temperature swings can affect metal finishes and fittings over time in those conditions it helps to use quality fittings in areas with direct exposure to air and moisture such as covered patios or near open windows consider corrosionresistant finishes or materials stainless steel powdercoated metals and some plastics will often hold up better than untreated metals choose enclosed or welldesigned fittings for bathrooms and outdooradjacent spaces where condensation can be a factor even purely decorative lights benefit from considering these details because a fixture that tarnishes quickly or traps moisture is not just an aesthetic issue it can become a maintenance problem the way natural daylight enters your home should guide your decorative lighting choices as well in rooms with strong afternoon sun you may want warmertoned lamps in the evening to restore a sense of calm after that bright light fades in rooms that never get much sun you can use slightly cooler white light in ceiling fixtures for clarity then soften it with warmwhite lamps at eye level to avoid a cold feeling colour temperature is an important piece of the coastal puzzle many coastalinspired spaces look best in the 2700k to 3000k range for living areas which reads as warm but not orange if your walls are white or offwhite this still looks fresh in work zones like kitchens a neutral 3000k to 4000k can keep surfaces looking clean while maintaining some warmth think about silhouette as well as style coastal lighting tends toward simple shapes domes cylinders globes or cleanlined lanterns these shapes create calm sightlines and keep the eye moving smoothly around the room they also tend to age well which matters because decorative lighting is not something most people want to replace every year in openplan spaces repeating one or two fixture styles helps tie the layout together for example similar glass pendants over an island and a related but not identical pendant over the dining table this repetition creates rhythm without feeling forced where futurefocused advice comes in is in planning control dimmers are often undervalued being able to dim coastalinspired fixtures lets you mimic dawn midday and dusk conditions in a subtle way early mornings and evenings lower light levels make textures and warm tones stand out daytime higher levels support tasks and keep spaces feeling lively if you are unsure where to start pick one room and ask a simple question what do i want this space to feel like at 8pm calm and quiet or social and bright once you define the mood you can select fixture materials colour temperature and brightness that move the room toward that feeling lighting specialists including the team at future light often begin a conversation with photos of your existing space and a description of how you actually use it from there it is easier to suggest whether you need more ambient light more task light or just a change in fixture style and colour temperature to achieve that coastal atmosphere the key idea is that coastal is not a theme it is a light quality if you focus on softness direction and material and then adjust for your climate and room usage you can arrive at a result that feels calm and connected to the coast without relying on obvious motifs

the world takes place on a planet similar to earth but slightly smaller it has a 27 axial tilt and a moon thats a bit larger and closer than ours which helps stabilize its rotation the planet orbits a white dwarf so overall it receives less light and heat the result is a world that feels colder and grayer many regions are dominated by constant rain damp climates and frequent snowfall its not a sunny or desertheavy planet its more a place of overcast skies wet ground and long harsh seasons technological level technology didnt progress the same way it did in our world for military social and cultural reasons global development is roughly on par with the late 1990s to early 2000s most major advances are concentrated in military and energy sectors while civilian life is more limited technologically the internet exists but it isnt open or global like ours the full network is mainly for military and government use while civilians only have access to a much more restricted and heavily monitored version this means information flow is controlled and propaganda plays a big role in society a geologically unstable planet the planet has intense tectonic activity multiple major plates mean that earthquakes tremors and volcanic activity are a normal part of life many volcanic regions arent constantly catastrophic but they strongly influence where people live which areas are wealthy and which territories become strategically important energy changes everything heres one of the biggest differences from our world energy uranium is extremely rare and located too deep to be exploited easily as a result nuclear energy never truly developed there are no major nuclear power plants and no nuclear weapons instead humanity pushed geothermal energy far beyond what weve achieved geothermal plants are highly advanced and capable of powering entire cities the problem is that they only work in volcanically or tectonically active regions and the infrastructure is extremely unequal agreements in this world geothermal energy fills the same strategic role oil had in ours suspicion and environmental weapons because the planet is already geologically unstable there are system is stuck in threat mode when youre chronically stressed your body stays in fight or flight dr emily nagoski researcher and author of burnout the secret to unlocking the stress cycle explains that stress isnt the problem its the incomplete stress cycle you experience the stressor brutal deadline shitty email existential dread about climate change but never signal to your body that youre safe now the stress hormones just accumulate your body thinks youre being chased by a lion 247 hence the racing heart digestive issues constant colds and brain fog that make you reread the same email 6 times physical signs youre ignoring your sleep is fucked but youre exhausted all day you get sick constantly because cortisol suppresses immune function you have zero appetite or youre stress eating everything random body pains tension headaches jaw clenching your emotions are either flatlined or you cry at dog videos check out the book when the body says no by dr gabor mat the dude spent decades studying the connection between stress and disease insanely good read thatll make you question everything you think you know about pushing through he shows how ignoring your bodys signals leads to serious health consequences its not woowoo its medical science how to actually complete the stress cycle this is the part that sounds stupid but works your body needs physical proof that the threat is over move your body intenselynot gentle yoga though that helps too i mean the kind of movement that makes you sweat and breathe hard go for a 20minute run do burpees and dance like an absolute maniac to 2000s emo music physical activity metabolizes stress hormones its literally biology do the stupid breathing thingyeah yeah everyone says breathe but box breathing 4 counts in 4 hold 4 out 4 hold actually activates your parasympathetic nervous system the app othership for guided breathwork sessions is designed by former athletes and feels less wellness influencer and more actual tool cry it out or laugh hardboth are biological stress releases watch a sad movie and let yourself ugly cry or find genuinely funny shit aunty donna sketches on youtube are solid your body doesnt care about your dignity it just wants the release the creativity cure nobody talks about dr stuart brown founder of the national institute for play spent his career researching play actual play not productive hobbies his research shows that playful activities rewire your stress response and rebuild cognitive flexibility started doing absolutely pointless creative stuff coloring books building lego learning card tricks zero productivity zero outcome goals just doing things for the sake of doing them i also discovered the app finch its a selfcare pet app that sounds childish but helps you build tiny habits without the pressure you take care of a little bird and it grows as you complete small wellness tasks way less intimidating than trying to overhaul your entire life for those wanting to go deeper
